🎯 Objectives

🎯 At the end of the learning experience, the learners should be able to:

  • Explain what fundamental skills are and distinguish locomotor movements from non-locomotor movements;
  • Identify and perform locomotor and non-locomotor movements correctly in different situations;
  • Participate actively and safely while showing control, awareness, and respect for others during movement activities.

Fundamental Skills

📘 📘 Meaning: Fundamental skills are basic movement abilities that learners use in physical activities, games, sports, and everyday actions. They help learners understand how the body moves and how to control movement safely. In this lesson, we focus on two important groups of fundamental movements: locomotor movements and non-locomotor movements.

Understanding the difference is simple: locomotor movements take the body from one place to another, while non-locomotor movements are performed mainly in one place without traveling to another location.

2 Fundamental Movements

🤸 There are two Fundamental Movements emphasized in this lesson:

1. Locomotor Movements
Movements that take the body from one place to another.
2. Non-Locomotor Movements
Movements performed mainly in one place without traveling to another location.

🚶 1. Locomotor Movements

📘 📘 Meaning: Locomotor movements are movements that move or transport the whole body from one place to another. The learner changes location while traveling through space. These movements may be done forward, backward, sideways, diagonally, or along a curved or straight pathway. Examples include walking, running, hopping, jumping, skipping, galloping, sliding, and leaping.

🌈 Example: A learner walks from a starting line to a cone, runs toward a finish line, hops across floor markers, or jumps forward over a line. These are locomotor movements because the learner's body travels to a different location.

🎬 Scenario: During a PE activity, Ana is standing behind a starting line while a cone is placed several meters in front of her. The teacher tells the class to reach the cone using a safe traveling movement. Ana begins by walking because the space in front of her is crowded. After a few seconds, the pathway becomes clearer, so she changes from walking to running. While moving toward the cone, she notices another learner crossing part of the pathway. Instead of running directly toward that learner, Ana slows down, changes her direction slightly, and follows a clear path around the person. Once the path is safe, she continues running until she reaches the cone. Ana changes her speed and direction during the activity, but the movement is still locomotor because her body keeps traveling from the starting point to another location.

🧍 2. Non-Locomotor Movements

📘 📘 Meaning: Non-locomotor movements are movements performed mainly while the body stays in the same general location. The learner can bend, stretch, twist, turn, sway, balance, curl, or move different body parts without traveling to another place. These movements help develop body control, stability, flexibility, and awareness.

🌈 Example: A learner bends down to touch the knees, twists the upper body while keeping the feet planted, stretches the arms overhead, sways from side to side, or holds a balance position. These are non-locomotor movements because the learner mainly stays in the same area.

🎬 Scenario: During a classroom movement activity, Ben is asked to stay inside a small marked circle while demonstrating different movements. First, he stretches both arms upward and slowly reaches toward the ceiling. Then he bends his knees and lowers his body without stepping outside the circle. Next, he twists his upper body to the left and right while keeping both feet planted. The teacher then asks him to sway gently from side to side, reach one arm forward, and finish by balancing in one position for five seconds. Ben is actively moving many parts of his body, but he remains inside the same marked area. The best classification is non-locomotor because the movements change his body position, shape, or direction without taking his body to another location.

Easy Way to Remember

LOCOMOTOR = GO
The body travels from one place to another.
NON-LOCOMOTOR = STAY
The body mainly stays in one place while changing position, shape, or direction.

Remember:

🤔 Ask yourself: Did the body travel to another place?

If yes, the movement is likely locomotor. If the body mainly stays in the same area while bending, stretching, twisting, turning, swaying, or balancing, it is non-locomotor.

💡 Fun Facts & Quick Knowledge

✨ Quick knowledge can help you connect the movement concepts you learned with real physical activities. Read each fact, then think about how you might see it during a game or movement task.

Movement Through History

There is no single person credited with discovering locomotor or non-locomotor movement. Humans have used basic movements throughout history because walking, running, jumping, bending, balancing, reaching, and turning are natural ways people interact with their environment. Over time, physical education systems developed ways to describe, classify, practice, and teach these movements so learners could understand how skills work and how they can be improved. This means movement skills are not inventions belonging to one person; they are human abilities that have been observed, practiced, organized, and taught across generations.

Movement Pathways

Traveling movements can use straight, curved, and zig-zag pathways. A straight pathway can be efficient when the route is clear, but it may not always be the safest or most useful option. A curved pathway can help a learner move around an obstacle, while a zig-zag pathway can require repeated changes of direction. Choosing a pathway involves thinking about the target, available space, other people, obstacles, and the amount of control needed. A good mover does not always choose the shortest route; the best pathway is often the one that fits the situation.

Movement Building Blocks

Fundamental movement patterns can become building blocks for more complex activities and sports. Running, jumping, balancing, throwing, catching, and striking may look simple when practiced separately, but they can become parts of longer and more demanding movement sequences. For example, a target activity may require a learner to run, stop, balance, position the body, and then throw. Practicing the basic skills gives learners a foundation they can combine and adapt when a new activity has different rules, equipment, distances, or space.

Skills Can Combine

A real activity can combine traveling, balancing, changing direction, and object control in one sequence. A learner may run toward a target, curve around an obstacle, stop under control, adjust body position, and then throw an object. This shows that movement concepts do not always appear one at a time. Good performance often requires several skills to work together, with the learner deciding which skill to emphasize as the situation changes. Thinking about the whole sequence helps learners understand why movement decisions matter.

Physical Literacy

Fundamental movement skills support physical literacy and participation in physical activities. Physical literacy involves developing the movement competence, confidence, motivation, and understanding needed to participate in physical activity. When learners become more comfortable with basic movements, they may feel more prepared to try new games, activities, and challenges. Practicing movement also gives learners opportunities to understand how their bodies respond to different tasks and how they can make safer and more effective decisions.

Target Games

Target-game situations often require learners to consider positioning, the relationship to an object, and how to send an object toward an intended area. A learner may need to decide where to stand, how far the target is, whether someone is blocking the pathway, and how much force to use. The most effective choice is not always the fastest choice. Learners often need to pause, observe, adjust their position, and then perform the object-control action with enough accuracy and control to meet the goal.

Challenge Game: Movement Detective

Directions: Read each situation carefully. Look at all the choices, then click the one answer that best solves the situation. Before choosing, think about the target, pathway, people, objects, available space, control, and safety.
